big: An open-ended debt fund promises that you can redeem on any working day. In April 2020 a fund house wound up six debt schemes after redemptions piled up on lower-rated bonds that would not sell. The promise is only as good as the assets behind it.

lines: Can I withdraw from a debt fund any day?
Normally yes, and the money arrives in a day or two. Let us watch what happens when everyone asks at once, and two funds hold different assets.

rows: Hard-to-sell bonds sold in a hurry (₹ crore)
alt: Two funds of 100 crore rupees meet a 20 crore redemption: one holds 40 crore in easy-to-sell assets, the other 5 crore
caps: Two funds of ₹100 crore. Fund P keeps ₹40 crore in cash and easy-to-sell bonds. Fund Q keeps ₹5 crore.
A scare hits. Investors ask for ₹20 crore back from each fund in a week.
P pays from its liquid ₹40 crore. Q has ₹5 crore, so it must sell ₹15 crore of hard-to-sell bonds.
In a hurry, buyers pay 5% less. Q's loss is ₹75 lakh, and the investors who stay bear it.
Daily liquidity is only as good as the assets behind it.

rows.name: After: main portfolio and side pocket

alt: A fund split into a main portfolio and a side pocket after one bond defaults
caps: A fund holds ₹100 crore. A bond worth 4% of it, ₹4 crore, hits a credit event such as a default.
The fund separates it. The healthy 96% stays in the main portfolio and carries on as before.
The troubled 4% goes into a side pocket. Every investor holds units in both.
Recoveries are paid to side pocket holders as they arrive.

title: What a side pocket does
stops: Separates the bond after a credit event
Brings every rupee back at once
Removes the loss from the books
alt: A shield with what a side pocket does and does not do
caps: A side pocket is a way to cope with a bad bond, not a repair.
It keeps the bad bond apart, so the main fund can carry on as normal.
It cannot make the bond good again. Recoveries come as they happen, and may be less than the loss.

q: Meena keeps ₹3 lakh of emergency money in a debt fund that holds mostly lower-rated papers because it yields 9%. Why does her adviser object?
opts: Lower-rated funds cannot be redeemed until the bonds mature
In stress it may sell hard-to-sell bonds at a loss when she needs cash
The yield would be taxed twice, once in the fund and once in her hands
Debt funds can never be sold in the first year after purchase
why: Open-ended funds can be redeemed on working days. The risk is a loss or limit in stress, not a fixed wait until maturity.
Lower-rated bonds can be hard to sell fast, so in a rush a fund may take losses or face limits when she needs cash.
Tax is charged once, on her gain. The adviser's worry is liquidity in stress, not double tax on the yield.
No general first-year bar exists on selling a debt fund. The risk is what happens when many sell together.

q: Fund Q sells ₹15 crore of hard-to-sell bonds at a 5% discount to meet redemptions. The investors who redeemed were paid the earlier NAV. Who carries the ₹75 lakh loss?
opts: Only the fund house, which must top it up from its own pocket
Nobody, since daily NAV averages the loss away
Those who redeemed, since their requests forced the sale
The investors who stay in the fund, as it lowers the NAV they hold
why: A fund house is not required to cover a fund's market losses. The loss falls on the unit holders.
NAV does not average a loss away. A sale at a discount reduces the fund's value for those who still hold units.
Redeemers already received their money at the earlier NAV. They are not charged for the sale afterwards.
Redeemers were paid at the earlier NAV. The discount from the forced sale falls on the units that remain.

q: A fund holds 4% in a bond that defaults, and creates a side pocket. Rohan holds ₹1,00,000 of units. What does he hold after that?
opts: Units in both: about ₹96,000 in the main portfolio and the rest in the side pocket
Only ₹96,000 in the main portfolio, as the ₹4,000 is written off
₹1,00,000 in the main portfolio, while the side pocket belongs to the fund house
₹96,000 in cash today, with the ₹4,000 returned next month
why: Investors hold units in both. The main portfolio carries on as before, and the side pocket pays out as recoveries arrive.
The side pocket is not a write-off. He still holds units in it, and recoveries from the bond are paid out to him.
The side pocket is owned by the investors, not the fund house. Each investor holds units in proportion to his old holding.
Nothing is paid in cash at the split. Units are created in both portfolios, and the side pocket pays only on recovery.

q: A client says SEBI regulates mutual funds, so she can always take her money out the next day. What is the honest reply?
opts: Only after a year, since all debt funds have a minimum holding period
Always yes, since SEBI guarantees redemption on the next working day
Normally yes, but stress can bring limits, so use liquid funds
Only if the fund house agrees, since redemption is at its discretion
why: Debt funds have no such general minimum. The risk is liquidity in stress, not a lock-in on every purchase.
SEBI regulates the rules but does not guarantee that a fund can pay out on a given day. April 2020 showed this.
Money normally arrives in a day or two. In extreme stress a fund can face limits, so emergency money goes in liquid or overnight funds.
Open-ended funds must accept redemptions. The fund cannot refuse at will, though stress can bring limits.

pts: Liquidity risk is real: a fund may not be able to sell a bond fast without a big price cut.
A side pocket separates a defaulted bond. Investors hold units in both, and recoveries are paid as they happen.
Emergency money belongs in liquid or overnight funds, not lower-rated ones.
